breadcrumb.name: Inverter AC vs Non-Inverter AC: Savings and Payback

sections.h2: Inverter AC vs non-inverter AC savings: where they come from
p: A non-inverter AC has one speed: its compressor runs at full power until the room reaches the setting, switches off, and starts again with a surge. An inverter AC slows its compressor down as the room cools and keeps it running gently, so it draws less on average. With the defaults the non-inverter AC averages 1.8 kW × 80% = 1.44 kW against 1 kW, which over 1,200 hours is 1,728 units against 1,200, a saving of 528 units a year.

Both average figures are planning values, not measurements of your units. The saving is largest in the hottest weeks, when the non-inverter compressor hardly ever switches off, and smaller in mild weather, when it cycles more; the second worked example shows the peak-summer case.

Payback = the extra price ÷ the saving a month. With the example price gap of Rs 40,000 and Rs 19,251 saved a year, that is about 24.9 calendar months, or about 13.7 if the compressor ran flat out every AC hour. The price gap is an example to show the method, not a market price; enter the gap between two real quotes for the same brand and tonnage.
The months are calendar months. The yearly saving already spreads the summer saving over the whole year, months with the AC off included, so do not count only the months the AC runs.

sections.h2: Is an inverter AC worth it?
p: Usually yes for a room cooled many hours a day at a high slab rate: the saving is largest where hours and tariff are both high. It is less clear for an AC used a few evenings a month or on the protected tariff, where the payback in the table below runs much longer.

Two benefits do not show in the payback: an inverter AC starts without a big surge, so it runs on a smaller generator, UPS or solar inverter, and it keeps the room at a steadier temperature. If you plan to run the AC on solar or a generator, that alone often decides it.

Repair costs differ: an inverter AC's control board is dearer to replace if it fails. Voltage swings shorten the life of both kinds; a stabiliser or a good surge protector protects either. The calculator does not count these because they vary too much to put a fair number on.

faq.q: How much electricity does an inverter AC save?
faq.a: With the planning averages here, about 528 units a year for a 1.5 ton AC run 1,200 hours, and up to about 960 units if every hour were like peak summer. Your figure depends on hours, weather and the models.

faq.q: What is the payback period of an inverter AC?
faq.a: The extra price ÷ the monthly saving. For the example gap of Rs 40,000, about 24.9 calendar months at Rs 36.46 per unit, longer at lower rates or fewer hours.

faq.q: Is an inverter AC worth it in Pakistan?
faq.a: Usually yes for long daily use at unprotected slab rates, where the payback is short. For a few hours a week or the protected tariff it takes much longer. Its soft start also helps on solar, UPS or a generator.

faq.q: Does an inverter AC save on solar?
faq.a: Yes, twice: it uses fewer units, and it starts without a big surge, so it needs a smaller solar inverter. See how many panels each kind needs with the solar panels for AC calculator.

faq.q: Why does a non-inverter AC use less than its rated power?
faq.a: Its compressor switches off when the room reaches the setting. Over a season it is on about 80% of each hour by our planning figure, so its average draw is below its running power; in the hottest weeks it hardly switches off and the inverter AC's advantage is largest.

faq.q: Is the price difference on this page real?
faq.a: No. Rs 40,000 is an example to show the sum, not a market price. Enter the gap between two real quotes for the same brand and tonnage.

key_facts: Yearly saving of an inverter AC = (non-inverter average kW − inverter average kW) × hours a year × tariff; payback in calendar months = the extra price ÷ (yearly saving ÷ twelve).

A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC draws 1.8 kW with its compressor on and about 80% of that over a season, 1.44 kW on average; against an inverter AC averaging 1 kW, 1,200 hours a year save about 528 units, Rs 19,251 at Rs 36.46 per unit.

In the hottest weeks, when the non-inverter compressor hardly switches off, the gap is wider: at that rate all year the same AC would save about 960 units and pay back in about 13.7 calendar months, so treat that as the optimistic end.
A home on the protected tariff at Rs 13.01 per unit takes about 69.9 calendar months to recover the same example price gap, because each saved unit is worth less.
mistakes: Comparing label watts. The inverter AC's label shows its maximum; the bill follows its average, about 1 kW for a 1.5 ton unit.
Comparing a non-inverter AC at full power with an inverter AC at its average. Both must be averages: the non-inverter compressor switches off for part of each hour.
Comparing different brands or tonnage. The price gap is fair only for the same brand, the same tonnage and the same installation.
Using the peak-summer saving all year. In the hottest weeks the gap is widest, as the second example shows; over a season it is smaller.

fields.name: kw_noninv
fields.label: Non-inverter AC power while running
fields.hint: Input watts from the label ÷ 1000, while the compressor is on. The default is a 1.5 ton non-inverter AC.

fields.name: duty
fields.label: Share of each hour the non-inverter compressor runs
fields.hint: Between 0 and 1. The default is the standard planning figure for a non-inverter AC averaged over the season; enter 1 for the hottest weeks, when the compressor hardly switches off.

fields.name: kw_inv
fields.label: Inverter AC average power
fields.hint: Average draw over an hour, not the maximum on the label. The default is the planning average for a 1.5 ton inverter AC; a plug-in energy meter gives your own.

fields.name: hours_year
fields.label: Hours the AC runs a year
fields.hint: Hours a day × days of AC weather, at most a full year of hours. The default is 8 hours a day for about five months; Karachi and southern Punjab often run more.

fields.name: tariff
fields.label: Electricity rate
fields.hint: Energy rate of your slab from the bill. The default is the Pakistan unprotected rate for 301 to 400 units a month.

fields.name: price_diff
fields.label: Extra price of the inverter model
fields.hint: Example figure, not a market price. Enter the gap between two real quotes for the same tonnage and brand, installation included.

examples.title: 1.5 ton AC at the planning average, 1,200 hours a year
examples.text: (1.44 − 1) kW × 1,200 h = 528 units × Rs 36.46 = Rs 19,251 a year. The example price gap of Rs 40,000 pays back in about 24.9 calendar months.

examples.title: Peak summer: the compressor never switches off
examples.text: In the hottest weeks the non-inverter AC runs at its full 1.8 kW. If every AC hour were like that, the saving would be 960 units, Rs 35,002 a year, and payback about 13.7 calendar months. Use it as the best case, not the average.

examples.title: Long hours: 2,400 hours a year
examples.text: An AC run day and night through a long summer saves 1,056 units, Rs 38,502 a year, and pays back the example gap in about 12.5 calendar months.

examples.title: Protected consumer at Rs 13.01 per unit
examples.text: The same units saved, 528 a year, are worth only Rs 6,869 at the protected rate, so the example gap takes about 69.9 calendar months. Note that an AC usually pushes a home past the protected limit.

content.answer: A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC averaging 1.44 kW uses about 1,728 units (Rs 63,003) in 1,200 hours a year; an inverter AC averaging 1 kW uses about 1,200 (Rs 43,752). The Rs 19,251 yearly saving pays back an extra Rs 40,000 in about 24.9 calendar months. Payback = extra price ÷ monthly saving.

formula.text: Payback (calendar months) = ΔPrice ÷ ((kW_non-inverter × duty − kW_inverter) × hours a year × tariff ÷ 12)
lines: kW_non-inverter = power of the non-inverter AC while its compressor runs
duty = share of each hour the compressor runs, averaged over the season
kW_inverter = average power of the inverter AC over an hour
hours a year = hours a day × days of AC use
tariff = Rs per unit of your slab
ΔPrice = extra price of the inverter model over the non-inverter one

content.safety: Both kinds of AC need their own circuit with the right cable and MCB; an AC on an overloaded socket can overheat the wiring. Have a licensed electrician check the circuit before installing a new AC.
